name: Mubami
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Mubami: OLAC lists only Swadesh list, transnewguinea.org lexicon, Ethnologue; no grammar or phonology found

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [page last modified 2024-06-25]. Mubami. NewGuineaWorld (Santa Fe Institute), UZH mirror.
sources.note: Phonology section marked 'under construction': 13 consonants, at least 5 vowels, no final consonants or clusters, historical notes on *k > ʔ, *n > l etc. Nothing on stress. Its comparative tables reproduce MacKenzie (2002) wordlist forms from Ugu/Kala, Parieme and Sogae villages that carry stress marks (ˈ and acute, e.g. o'meto, gu'tɑle, ɑmɑ́), i.e. someone transcribed stress in the field, but no rule is stated. Sources listed: Franklin 1973: 270-273; Franklin ed. 1973: 577-578; Franklin 1975: 264-268; Reesink 1976; Reesink n.d. survey vocabulary; MacKenzie 2002 (176 terms, 19 phrases).

sources.citation: Reesink, Ger P. 1976. Languages of the Aramia River Area. In Reesink, Fleischmann, Turpeinen & Lincoln (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 19, 1-37. Pacific Linguistics A-45. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A45.1
sources.note: Section 6 Tao-Suamato (pp. 18-21); 6.3 'Notes on Phonology and Grammar' (p. 21) gives 16 consonants (p, t, k, ʔ, b, d, g, m, n, v, s, ɣ, h, r, w, y) and 5 vowels, pronoun set, three tenses and word order; nothing on stress, accent, tone or syllable structure. The only stress remark in the paper ('Vowels seem to be lengthened when they occur in stressed syllables, stress being probably phonemic', p. 10) is in 4.3 on Bainapi, a different language.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. (ed.) 1973. The Linguistic Situation in the Gulf District and Adjacent Areas, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-26. 622 pp. (Appendix G.3 'Tao Suamato' 100-item wordlist, pp. 577-578; rearranged as Z'graggen 1975)
sources.note: Only a raw 100-item wordlist for Tao-Suamato (pp. 577-578); the apostrophes in forms such as goloʔi, muʔi, seiʔi are glottal stops, not stress marks. The volume's stress statements (pp. 30-33, 82, 114, 250 etc.) all concern other languages (Angan, Kiwaian, Kewah). No stress statement for Tao-Suamato/Mubami anywhere in the volume.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1973. Other Language Groups in the Gulf District and Adjacent Areas. In K. J. Franklin (ed.), The Linguistic Situation in the Gulf District and Adjacent Areas, Papua New Guinea, 263-277. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: 7.44 Tao-Suamato (pp. 270-271): location, villages, population, lexicostatistics. 7.46 'Comments on Phonology and Grammar' (p. 272): phonemes common to the three Inland Gulf languages, six sound correspondences, pronoun table. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid muba1238 (Hammarström, Forkel, Haspelmath & Bank)
sources.note: Five overview references (Franklin 1973, Ross 1995, Z'graggen 1975, Reesink 1976, Lean 1986); zero grammar/phonology/sketch references. No stress information.

sources.citation: Greenhill, Simon J. TransNewGuinea.org, language page 'Mubami'
sources.note: 206 lexical items from Franklin 1973 and Reesink 1976 (a few Franklin items show an acute, e.g. domóge 'cold'); no phonology or stress statement.
Consonant and vowel tables attributed to Reesink 1976; nothing on stress.
